legend: Hacker Kirill decided to develop a new random number generator. To do this, he took two large numbers n$$$ n $$$ and m$$$ m $$$, turned them into powers of two, added them up, and raised the resulting amount to a small power of k$$$ k $$$, and got some number r=(2n+2m)k$$$ r = (2^n + 2^m)^k $$$. Random numbers were supposed to be cut from the binary notation of the number r$$$ r $$$.

When Kirill posted his ideas on the forum, one of his colleagues said that the numbers obtained would be too non-random, pointing out that even just the number of ones in the binary representation in the number r$$$ r $$$ is too predictable.

Help Kirill verify his colleague's statement. Write a program that uses the numbers n$$$ n $$$, m$$$ m $$$ and k$$$ k $$$ to determine the number of ones in the binary representation of the number r=(2n+2m)k$$$ r = (2^n + 2^m)^k $$$.
input: The single line contains 3 integers n(0≤n≤109)$$$ n (0 \leq n \leq 10^9) $$$, m(0≤m≤109)$$$ m (0 \leq m \leq 10^9) $$$ and k(0≤k≤100)$$$ k (0 \leq k \leq 100) $$$, separated by a space.
output: In a single line, print a number – the amount of ones in the binary representation of the number r=(2n+2m)k$$$ r = (2^n + 2^m)^k $$$.
